The benchmark code is public (go-client-server-benchmarks: benchmarks_test.go, cmdstream_test.go, grpc_test.go; go.mod pins grpc v1.80.0), and the README states Go 1.24.1, the exact go test commands and the Ryzen 7 PRO 5850U CPU.

corrections.caveats: The benchmark repo (ymz-ncnk/go-client-server-benchmarks, 17 stars) is maintained by the cmd-stream author, so it is not independent. Methodology, code, Go version and CPU are fully disclosed, so it stays at tier A. The run is on a single laptop, not a controlled server, and no variance is reported beyond -count=10. The comparison is cmd-stream over raw TCP against gRPC over HTTP/2. The protobuf codec on cmd-stream also beats gRPC (108788 vs 46142 QPS at 1 client), so most of the gain comes from the transport, not from the MUS codec. The fixed-count run (100,000 requests, sec.csv) shows a smaller gap: 0.612s vs 2.091s at 1 client (~3.4x) and 0.383s vs 1.033s at 16 clients (~2.7x).

tier_reason: The 2021 run is fully disclosed. The post gives CPU, Go 1.16.6, versions of every framework (rpcx 1.6.5, grpc 1.39.0), the exact server/client commands and a raw data table: rpcx 249,308-317,874 TPS against grpc 96,463-136,108. corrections.claimed_speedup: ~2.3x-2.6x higher throughput than grpc-go 1.39.0 across 100-5000 concurrent clients (249,308 vs 96,463 TPS at 100; 303,287 vs 116,608 at 1000; 317,874 vs 136,108 at 2000; 315,397 vs 121,989 at 5000), and ~1.3x-1.5x over the Go standard library net/rpc (249,308 vs 189,221 at 100; 315,397 vs 204,503 at 5000) (derived from page data: the raw-data table image data.png on the 2021 post)
corrections.baseline: gRPC (grpc-go 1.39.0); also Go standard library net/rpc (Go 1.16.6)
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Go 1.16.6; rpcx 1.6.5, grpc 1.39.0, go std rpc 1.16.6, kitex 0.0.3, arpc 1.1.5; run as ./xxx_server -d 127.0.0.1:8972 and ./xxx_client -c <concurrency> -n 10000000 -s 127.0.0.1:8973 (go build flags not stated)
corrections.hardware: Intel Xeon Silver 4110 @ 2.10GHz, 2 sockets (the post states 8 physical cores and 32 logical cores with hyper-threading), 128GB RAM; client and server on the same machine over loopback
corrections.workload: Synchronous RPC with a 581-byte Protobuf BenchmarkMessage: the server sets one field to OK and returns it. Client and server run on the same machine over loopback, with a shared client pool and warmup. Each scenario sends 10,000,000 requests at 100/200/500/1000/2000/5000 concurrent clients, with no simulated processing delay.
corrections.caveats: All results are first-party: the rpcx author runs the benchmark and publishes it on his blog, colobu.com. The rounds in the same benchmark project disagree. The 2018 chart (Go 1.9.0, E5-2630 v3; linked from the rpcx README) shows ~1.5x over grpc-go (~205k/199k/200k vs ~135k/131k/129k calls/s at 500/2000/5000 clients) and ~2.7-2.9x over Thrift (~75k/70k/72k). In that round the Go standard library net/rpc (~290k) beat rpcx. The 2019 table in the rpcx-ecosystem/rpcx-benchmark README has grpc ahead at 256 concurrency (130,642 vs 122,166 TPS) and rpcx only ~1.15x ahead at 512/1024. The 2020 test_data.md has grpc ahead at c=100 (108,928 vs 100,926) and rpcx 1.30x ahead at c=1000 (171,600 vs 132,037). The size of the gap therefore depends heavily on the round, the hardware and the concurrency. The 2021 numbers are in an image table only. HEAD of rpcxio/rpcx-benchmark has since moved to grpc v1.48.0 and rpcx v1.8.33, so reproducing the exact run needs commit 699aab8d. GitHub's license API reports NOASSERTION, but the LICENSE file is the standard Apache License 2.0 notice (Copyright 2017 Chao yuepan).

tier_reason: The README table matches the record exactly: 232,712 vs 227,973, 232,072 vs 224,498, 231,135 vs 222,493 and 222,578 vs 216,833 msg/s. corrections.workload: Plaintext WebSocket echo server driven by the uSockets load_test client from the denoland/fastwebsockets benches harness. Payloads are 512 and 1024 bytes at 100 and 500 concurrent connections, measured in messages/sec. These cases are not in the published run.js, which uses 20B/100, 1KB/10 and 16KB at 10/200/500, so a locally modified harness was used.
corrections.caveats: The margin over uWebSockets is only 2-3%, which is within plausible run-to-run noise for a single-machine run. No repeated runs or variance are reported. The numbers are self-reported and have not changed since the repo's initial commit (2025-12-29), while the library has since gone from v1.x to v2.1.0. The harness is third-party (denoland/fastwebsockets benches), but the sockudo-ws target, its echo server and the modified cases are not published, so the run cannot be reproduced as stated. The environment line (Ryzen 9 7950X, Linux 6.18, Rust 1.82) was added after the numbers. Rust 1.82 cannot compile this edition-2024 crate. No build flags for either side are given.
